title: Jay McShan's Kansas City feel
summary: Durham praises McShan's tempo sense and riffs as underrated, comparing him on piano to T-Bone Walker on guitar.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, there's one other thing about Kansas City I was going to say. What about -- I mean, Jay McShan, he has -- now, he has a sort of a pretty unique feeling, too, I always think. I always think he's very much underrated. He's -- it isn't quite like Basie's, but he does have a feeling for swing, doesn't he?
Yes, sir, he has that Western idea of getting that tempo down right.
And not of overexecuting. And the riffs he sets are still riffs that you can write songs from.
But they got a lot of them up East here that you can't write no songs from. I'll tell you, man.

Yes. Do you think that -- it's one of my theories that the fact that he got Charlie Parker to New York in his band, that's all they ever have to say about Jay McShan; that Charlie Parker came to New York and he's --
Well, I think -- it's sleeping a little bit.

It's sleeping on him a little bit. He's original man, and he offers a good feeling and everything, and he's playing his thing. He's a T-bone walker on the piano just like T-bone on the guitar, Christian was -- yeah, because Christian picked up -- he moved on into the Eastern style along with (unintelligible). And it wasn't nobody else playing it, so --
It's a sort of rhythmic gift, essentially, isn't it?
